commentary_title: Freight rates fail to catch up to trade activity
commentary_summary: The tonne miles index increased slightly in week 5 to end at 93.3 despite a fall in the %laden in both the East and the West. There was an uptick in tonnage enquiries in the Middle East and West Africa leading to a slight uptick in rates. | Refinery maintenance kept trade activity low in the US Gulf and Latin America which weighed on freight rates. However, there is an anticipation for tonnage demand to pick up in week 6 which could push up rates on routes towards the East. | There was an increase in the tonnage build-up around China which is likely a result of the bad weather at the ports coupled with the upcoming Lunar New Year curbing trade activity.

commentary_title: Subdued market activity could persist next week
commentary_summary: The tonne-miles index continued to increase last week from its upturn in week 4 to end the week at 10.5 points. The crude market had a quiet week leading to the softening of rates on most routes. AG-China route declined by $3/day in week 9. | Weak tonnage demand in the East led to a few vessels ballasting West in the hopes of higher activity next week. Muted demand in the USG is likely to continue next week while more ballasters are travelling Westbound. This could lead to rates softening further in week 10. | The global ballast and laden speed declined in both the East and the West as activity in the crude market waned. Due to more vessels heading westward, congestion eased up in Chinese ports, leading to tonnage gathering in the Atlantic.

commentary_title: Tonne-miles index touches new high in 2024
commentary_summary: The VLCC tonne-miles index reached 109.8 in week 13, the highest so far this year. It was higher by 19.3 points YoY as tensions in the Red Sea have continued to push out vessels on longer routes. | There was a continued rise in the %laden in the West likely as a result of US demand beginning to head towards a recovery post refinery maintenance. Meanwhile, activity remained firm in ex-Brazil with several tonnage expected to head towards China in the next few weeks. | Rates on TD3C and TD22 did see a decline in the previous week but East-bound routes are likely to pick up in week 14 as more tonnage prepares to head East.

commentary_title: Asian demand leads trade in week 17
commentary_summary: It was a softer week in the VLCC segment with the tonne-miles index falling by 1.2 points to reach 113 in week 17. Trade was weaker in the West of Suez causing freight rates to fall marginally on most routes. | While vessels had a hard time fixing cargoes from West Africa, MEG to Asia trade remained buoyant which helped in cushioning freight rates on most MEG to Asia routes. | The global ballast and laden speed dipped last week mainly as a result of vessels slowing down in the East. This could indicate a softening of trade next week especially towards the Indian West Coast regions. Trade in the West could firm up next week supporting freight rates.

commentary_title: Muted demand across the board weighs on freight rates
commentary_summary: it was another lacklustre week for VLCC as freight rates continued to decline on most of the major routes. Nonetheless, the stretched voyages pushed up the tonne-miles index to 110.4 points, gaining 4 points over the week. | The global laden and ballast speed declined further in week 22 as tonnage demand weakened in the Middle East and the US. VLCC activity in West Africa also remained muted and is likely to remain weak in the short term as market indicators do not point towards any signs of a recovery in activity. | The tonnage underway in the East saw an uptick amid a declining %laden likely indicating that market activity will remain soft as more ballast vessels await to be fixed. Meanwhile, the charter rates will likely continue to follow the downward trend.

commentary_title: The lull in demand for large tankers likely to prevail
commentary_summary: The tonne-miles index increased slightly in week 27 despite weak market activity dampening the tonnage demand for VLCCs. The MEG to West Coast India was the only route that had its freight rates stabilised throughout the week. | There is some growing traction towards the Suezmax segment which added to weaker demand for the larger carriers. Tonnage underway towards the East especially saw continued decline amid the waning demand. | Subdued VLCC demand is likely to remain in week 27 with the tonnage underway in the East continuing to decline. Some respite might come from the USG-Caribs route.

commentary_title: VLCC demand continues to be buoyed by China
commentary_summary: The VLCC tonne-miles index ended the week at 108.5 points. Apart from a slight dip in week 25, it has been on a continuous rise as demand especially towards the East has been positive. Following the positive trend, week 30 also saw the market strengthening, bumping up rates on the MEG-China route. | There was great enthusiasm for VLCC tonnage at the start of the week but waned towards the end as markets in the Atlantic showed progressively weaker interest. Week 31 is likely to retain these weakened sentiments in the Westbound trade. | The West Africa to China trade also seems hopeful for next week which will further support freight rates in the East.

commentary_title: Positive week for VLCCs despite despite a fall in tonne-miles
commentary_summary: The VLCC tonne-miles index fell further in week 33 ending the week at 112 points. Despite the decline, the freight rates increased on most routes as plenty of cargo was available, boosting the tonnage demand. | The crude trade towards the East was robust, especially in the second half of the week. The Arabian Gulf to India/China routes saw some big gains in rates as the week went by. The positive sentiments are likely to remain in week 34 as well. | Firm crude demand in Asia has also had a positive impact on US Gulf to East routes. Even ex-Brazil rates saw a rise which is likely to attract more ballasters in week 35 along the Eastrn Coastlines. VLCC demand as a whole is likely to remain firm next week.

commentary_title: VLCC demand to improve soon
commentary_summary: The VLCC tonne-miles Index declined further in week 36 after falling since week 31 except for a slight upturn last week. The index ended the week at 104.2 points, just about a point higher YoY. Nevertheless, the crude market is at the eve of a comeback as the winter demand will soon drive up tonnage demand. | Asian demand especaialy on ex-MEG routes improved in August and is expected to continue rising. This will help boost VLCC demand improving tonne-miles and utilisation alike. | There seems to be a positive sentiment in the market which is likely to be reflected from next week onwards with an uptick in rates. The vessel movement has also been increasing which will increase the underway tonnage in week 27.

commentary_title: VLCC markets remain subdued but hopeful
commentary_summary: The VLCC market started off with high sentiments, which phased out towards the end of the week. The tonne-miles index weakened, ending the week at 101.3 points. The markets in the Far East could see further softening next week as the Golden Week celebrations are already around the corner. However, they could see a revival once the celebrations end. | Firm demand was observed in the US-Latin America routes, but hurricanes have remained a deterrent to trade in the US Gulf regions. Meanwhile, West African markets remain positive despite a subdued week, as winter demand is expected to soon drive up tonnage demand.

commentary_title: Weak Asian demand to keep VLCC rates soft
commentary_summary: The VLCC tonne-miles index declined for a third consecutive week ending at 102.5 points, lower by close to 4 points. There is weakness in the tonnage demand, especially towards the East, where a lower-than-expected Chinese demand is hampering trade for the winter months. The TD3C route also declined further and is likely to remain weak even in the next week. | Markets started out slow but gained some momentum towards the middle of the week towards the West of Suez. The MEG to UKC route saw an uptick in rates as an increase in cargoes resulted in a requirement for more tonnage. The market activity for next week however seems to be on the grimmer side due to the possibility of the weakness in the smaller size segments weighing down on VLCC rates.

commentary_title: Freight rates weaken over increased tonnage supply
commentary_summary: The VLCC tonne-mile index improved slightly in week 48 as the %laden towards the West saw an uptick with several tonnage being fixed in the previous weeks. | Freight rates on the other hand saw a big dip on most major routes especially in the AG as surplus tonnage gathered in the region. The ex-USG routes also saw a decline in activity with Thanksgiving week dampening trade in the region. West Africa and Brazil to China saw a relatively busier week. | The market activity next week is likely to remain soft, weighing on the freight rates. Some improvement might be seen towards the West as the markets in the West Coast Atlantic regions resume activity.

commentary_title: Pre-Christmas rush firms up activity in the MEG
commentary_summary: The VLCC tonne-miles index declined in week 51, ending the week at 103.4 points. Fleet utilisation has also been declining in recent weeks as the holiday season dampened market activity, especially in the West of Suez. The East side markets look brighter, with some vessels being fixed on ex-MEG to Asia, likely due to a pre- Christmas rush before the year ends. The relatively stronger activity in the MEG could see rates firm up next week as tonnage supply has contracted in the regions. | Softness in the market has slowed the average speed of laden vessels while the speed of ballast vessels remained intact. A lack of a year-end rush across markets is likely to weaken the vessels underway in the next week.

commentary_title: Fresh US sanctions causes frenzy in the VLCC tanker market
commentary_summary: The VLCC-tonne miles index declined last week ending the week at 96.7 points as tonnage demand had been weak in the previous week with less vessels moving underway. | Freight rates on the other hand soared up as the US rolled up with fresh sanction on two major Russian insurers causing mayhem in the oil and tanker markets. Freight rates shot up on most routes even for the smaller tanker segments with routes towards the UKC seeing the highest surge. | The vessel utilisation is likely to increase next week with freight rates continuing to hover around the new levels.

commentary_title: US tariffs continue to keep VLCC rates high
commentary_summary: The VLCC tonne-miles index fell slightly in week 6 ending the week at 99.7 points. Nevertheless, freight rates surged on most routes, especially on those headed towards China which increased by around 30% since the past week. Tonnage movement has been more active towards the West due to US' sanctions on Russian crude getting more stringent. | The MoM decline in vessels in port in the West declined by about 30%, as a lot of trade potential wore off during the week. Despite this, the weakness in tonnage supply continued to keep freight rates afloat.

commentary_title: VLCC rates decline as tonnage builds up
commentary_summary: The VLCC tonne-miles index ended at 100.8 points, down 2.5 points from the previous week as market activity waned as the week progressed. Despite the week starting out firm, rates fell as activity levels declined, likely due to the International Energy week drowning out trade sentiments. | As a result, there seems to be a buildup in tonnage, which is likely to keep rates flattened next week. The speed for both laden and ballast vessels increased last week, however, which could see even more buildup towards the Atlantic West as more ballast vessels head West.

commentary_title: Low tonnage supply to keeps freight rates high
commentary_summary: The VLCC tonne-miles index reached a new high this year, ending week 12 at 106.4 points. Rates have been firming up overall, especially towards the West, as new geopolitical events unfold and the US clamps down on more vessels involved in trading sanctioned crude. | A surge in the %laden towards the West leading to a decline in tonnage supply, is likely to keep freight rates firm next week on ex- USG routes. | An uptick in vessels at port in the East could keep rates sideways next week while ballast vessels heading towards the MEG increase.

commentary_title: Weakness prevails in the VLCC market
commentary_summary: The VLCC tonne-miles index weakened slightly in week 15, down by 0.6, as market tonnage demand continued to be soft. Despite expectations of an improvement in demand and rates at the start of the month, sentiments have quietened down, while tonnage seems to be building up in both the East and the West. | There was an uptick in activity toward West Africa, but this did not translate to an upward movement in freight rates. Markets are likely to remain weak in week 16, especially towards the West as tonnage amid the decline in tonnage underway.

commentary_title: Markets in the AG weaken while it firms up in the USG
commentary_summary: It was a slow week for the VLCC market. Market sentiments weakened, causing the tonne-miles index to decline 7 points, ending the week at 102.8. Vessel speeds slowed, especially towards the West, while freight rates weakened slightly. | There was ample activity towards the USG as tonnage demand improved due to an increase in the volume of cargoes. A slow buildup of the available tonnage in the region leaves potential for rates to firm up next week.

commentary_title: VLCC freight rates to remain elevated
commentary_summary: The escalation of conflict in the Middle East has brought new geopolitical upheavals in the tanker market. While the VLCC market was soft for most of week 24, the Israel-Iran conflict resulted in a sudden uptick in tanker rates towards the end of the week. As the Strait of Hormuz is a hub for VLCC trade, freight rates will likely remain heightened as long as the conflict persists. | Meanwhile, vessels might avoid the region due to increased risks caused by the conflict. In the short term, this could cause more vessels to ballast towards other regions, resulting in higher tonne- miles covered.

commentary_title: Seasonal weakness in demand weighs on VLCC freight
commentary_summary: The VLCC tonne miles index fell in week 27 ending at 97.1 points. The VLCC market seems to have been affected by the seasonal weakness in demand as freight rates declined on most routes. After the brief surge in rates during mid-June due to the Israel-Iran conflict, rates have been on the decline. With a seasonal lull ahead, weak tonnage demand will continue weigh on freight rates. | The %laden in the East declined while it increased marginally towards the West. However, with tonnage underway declining on both sides, market activity will remain weak in week 28.

commentary_title: Uptick in Eastbound tonnage demand to support rates
commentary_summary: It was a quiet week for the crude tanker market as market sentiments weakened and excess tonnage supply, especially in the Middle East, softened rates. However, the VLCC tonne-miles index improved, ending the week at 100.7 points owing to increased movement towards the East. | Despite spot rates declining on ex-MEG, rates towards China showed an uptick last week, which is likely to result in a higher utilisation and increased %laden vessels in the East next week.

commentary_title: Weak demand to weigh on VLCC rates in the East
commentary_summary: The VLCC tonne-miles index remained stable at around 100.1 points in week 35. The global ballast speed declined last week, as vessel speeds slowed down towards the West amid increased traffic at the ports. | Tonnage demand in the MEG-East weakened last week which is expected to weigh on freight rates. | Towards the West, ex-USG route rates saw an uptick as tonnage supply was tight. There is likely to be an increase in underway ballast vessels next week.

commentary_title: Freight rates improve in both the East and the West
commentary_summary: The VLCC tonne-miles index remained stable at around 105.9 points in week 38. Meanwhile, the speed in the West has risen for both ballast and laden vessels, while vessel speeds in the East have slowed down. | Rates firmed up in both the East and the West with vessel loadings towards China seeing an uptick last week. | There were positive gains on both the ex-MEG and ex-USG routes last week. However, there could be a slight softening in rates next week.

commentary_title: Asian holidays weaken market spirits
commentary_summary: The VLCC tonne-miles index declined in week 41 ending the week at 108.3 points. Holidays in China and South Korea led to dampened demand and weakness in rates. | Vessel speeds also slowed down, consequently, in both the East and the West, but %laden vessels saw an uptick. | Market activity is likely to remain low next week but could rise towards the end, leaving freight rates sideways.

commentary_title: VLCC freight rates reach an unexpected peak in week 44
commentary_summary: The VLCC tonne-miles index surged to a new high in week 44, reaching 113.8 points. It was a phenomenal week for the tanker segment as freight rate gains reached new peaks. | The AG-China route, in particular, saw rates surge as tonnage demand increased throughout the week. The utilisation for VLCCs also firmed, and the momentum is expected to continue next week as well. | The recent US sanctions on major Russian oil producers will bode well for the Middle Eastern oil suppliers, boosting the MEG to Asia tonne-mile demand.

commentary_title: Strong VLCC momentum persists but geopolitical shifts introduce caution to tonne-mile outlook
commentary_summary: The VLCC tonne-miles index climbed to 110.6 in week 47, marking one of its highest readings of the year. Although slightly below the week 44 peak of 113.8, it still reflects strong long-haul crude movements and sustained demand for VLCC capacity. | VLCC rates rose sharply helped by a tight supply of ships and steady fixing of late-November and early-December cargoes. MEG–China rates moved up and ex-USG levels also improved. Product tankers, especially LR2s, also gained support from the firm crude market. | The prospect of a Russia-Ukraine peace deal has shifted market sentiment, as the possibility of eased sanctions points to shorter Russian trade routes and a looser supply backdrop softening the tonne-mile support that had benefited VLCCs during the sanctions period.

commentary_title: VLCC market softens as demand stays quiet
commentary_summary: The VLCC tonne-miles index declined in week 50. Fleet utilisation currently stands at 91.3%. | Global laden speeds rose during the week in contrast to a slight decline in global ballast speeds. The proportion of eastbound laden voyages fell in week 50 while westbound laden voyages increased. | Both the Arabian Gulf and West Africa VLCC markets remained relatively quiet with limited chartering enquiries. Market direction in the near term will depend on whether demand improves in the coming weeks.

commentary_title: VLCC utilisation stable but momentum weakens on idle build-up
commentary_summary: VLCC utilisation stood at 89.2%, up slightly by 0.6 percentage points week-on- week, though still 1.1 percentage points below last year, indicating the market remains somewhat softer on a yearly basis.Spot earnings on the benchmark TD3C route hovered around 476 WS, showing that while rates have eased from recent peaks, they continue to hold at relatively firm levels. | Even though bunker prices have dropped sharply, VLCC speeds have only adjusted modestly and vary by region, suggesting that subdued crude demand and excess vessel capacity—not fuel costs—are currently shaping the movement of ships. | Rising ballast tonnage at anchor in the West and increasing idle vessels highlight a build-up of prompt tonnage near load regions (US Gulf, West Africa). | The increase in ballast vessels in regions like the Atlantic and China suggests that ships are struggling to find their next cargo, leading to longer idle times and a sustained excess of available tonnage in the market.

commentary_title: Resilient Asian import demand and Atlantic exports support VLCC activity
commentary_summary: VLCC utilisation stood at 89.6% indicating stronger vessel employment as more ships moved from waiting positions into active trading. Underlying demand remained supported by long-haul crude movements from the Atlantic Basin to Asia. Tonne-mile index remained above the annual baseline at 103.3 and was 7.3% higher than a year ago, indicating that voyage distances continue to support vessel demand. | Asian demand remained relatively resilient. Chinese discharge activity stabilised after recent weakness, while India continued to demonstrate steady crude import requirements. The Pacific region maintained healthy levels of laden vessel activity, reinforcing Asia's role as the primary demand centre for VLCCs. | Continued crude exports from the US Gulf, Brazil and West Africa, combined with stable Asian import requirements, helped maintain a favourable demand environment for VLCCs.

commentary_title: Atlantic Basin congestion continues to absorb prompt VLCC tonnage and support freight rates.
commentary_summary: The VLCC market remained firm, as utilisation stood at 90.8% despite slowdown in tonne-mile demand. With the tonne-mile index falling to 82.2, the persistence of strong vessel employment highlights the role of congestion, vessel positioning inefficiencies and tighter effective supply in underpinning freight market performance. | Effective VLCC supply remained constrained by persistent congestion particularly across the Atlantic Basin. A sharp increase in western anchorage volumes, combined with higher global tonnage waiting at anchor, continued to absorb available capacity and support spot freight markets. | Asia continued to underpin global VLCC activity, with China, India and the broader Pacific Basin accounting for the largest concentration of both laden and ballast tonnage. While congestion at key discharge hubs has eased from the elevated levels seen earlier in the year, anchorage volumes remain above historical averages, reflecting sustained crude import demand across the region.

commentary_title: VLCC utilisation strengthened despite improving vessel availability,
commentary_summary: VLCC utilisation strengthened to 91.9% during the week, remaining above the long-term equilibrium level despite signs of rising vessel availability. A modest recovery in the tonne-mile index and a higher share of laden vessels in the East indicate that crude trade demand remained sufficiently resilient to absorb available tonnage and support overall fleet employment. | East of Suez continued to underpin market fundamentals, although signs of easing tightness emerged. The proportion of laden vessels increased, reflecting healthy cargo activity, but underway tonnage fell sharply while anchored tonnage rose substantially. This suggests that vessel availability around major Middle East loading areas is rebuilding as cargo growth struggles to keep pace with fleet positioning. | Congestion across major Asian discharge hubs eased further, particularly in China. Laden tonnage at anchor in China declined sharply while Indian discharge-side congestion remained well below earlier peaks. The reduction in waiting times removed an important supply constraint and contributed to the recovery in effective fleet productivity observed across the VLCC market.

commentary_title: VLCC utilisation strengthens despite weak tonne-mile dmeand
commentary_summary: VLCC utilisation improved to 92.3% in week 40, up 1.6 percentage points MoM and YoY, suggesting stronger fleet employment despite subdued demand indicators. However, the tonne-mile index remained weak at 87.5, down 2.2% YoY, suggesting that reduced voyage distances and softer long-haul crude movements continue to weigh on underlying transport demand. | Market activity showed signs of regional divergence, with vessel capacity at anchor declining by 4.1% MoM in the west and 0.5% in the east. Higher ballast speeds in the east point to active fleet repositioning and improving vessel availability, while the recovery in the tonne-mile index from recent lows indicates some improvement in cargo flows heading into the fourth quarter. | Easing congestion and faster vessel turnaround continued to lift effective fleet supply. Lower anchorage levels, combined with elevated ballast and laden sailing speeds, increased tonnage availability across key trading regions, offsetting support from stronger utilisation and limiting the upside for VLCC freight rates despite firmer bunker prices.

commentary_title: VLCC utilisation strengthens despite weaker tonne-mile demand
commentary_summary: VLCC utilisation rose to 93.7% in Week 43, up 2.5 percentage points MoM and YoY, indicating significantly tighter fleet employment. However, the tonne-mile index remained subdued at 91.7, down 17.4% YoY, suggesting that shorter-haul crude movements and weaker long-haul trade flows continue to weigh on underlying transport demand despite the recent recovery from mid-year lows. | Higher fleet employment was driven by stronger vessel deployment, with the share of laden vessels declining by 1.6 percentage points MoM in the East and 3.3 percentage points in the West, while the proportion of vessels underway increased and in-port tonnage fell sharply. At the same time, anchored capacity declined by 46.0% MoM in the West and 1.5% in the East, indicating improved vessel circulation and reduced congestion across key trading regions. | Market tightness remained broadly balanced as stronger utilisation was partially offset by improving fleet productivity. Ballast speeds increased by 6.2% MoM in the East and 8.1% in the West despite bunker prices rising 8.6% MoM to $933/tonne, while laden anchor days increased 3.2% on a four-week moving-average basis.
